title: The Terrorism Threat to the 2026 Midterm Elections: What the Data Tells Us
gist: Using the CSIS U.S. Terrorism Incidents Dataset, the brief finds only 11 election-related terrorist incidents from 2015 to mid-2026 — 10 of them since 2021 — from across the political spectrum, mostly lone actors with firearms, and none killed their intended victims. For the 2026 midterms the threat spans the whole election cycle, with jihadist, anti-government/partisan, accelerationist and Middle East-linked identity grievances as plausible drivers; the authors urge a proportionate security response that does not chill participation or civil liberties.

themes.theme: Frequency and trend of election terrorism

insights.claim: Only 11 of hundreds of U.S. terrorist attacks and plots between January 2015 and June 2026 were election-related, but 10 of the 11 occurred in 2021 or later, spanning the 2020, 2022 and 2024 cycles.
insights.so_what: Election-related terrorism may be rising, but the small sample means the trend is suggestive, not definitive.
insights.quote: 10 of the 11 incidents occurred in 2021 or later
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Terrorists have targeted U.S. elections in each of the past several cycles, making similar violence around the 2026 midterm elections possible though still a tiny share of overall U.S. terrorism.
insights.so_what: Tail-risk of political violence around the midterms is non-trivial and could affect political stability perceptions.
insights.locator: The IssueTerrorism aimed directly at U.S.
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: The study excludes the 2024 Butler, Pennsylvania attempt on Donald Trump (no ideological motive found) and the 2025 assassination of Minnesota legislator Melissa Hortman (not election-connected), so it understates the broader climate of political violence.
insights.so_what: Narrow terrorism counts are an incomplete gauge of political-violence risk around elections.
insights.locator: What Is Not Included Here and Why
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Election terrorists fall into three motive groups: overturning results viewed as fraudulent (6 incidents, incl. Solomon Peña's four shootings and January 6 actors), assassinating disliked candidates (3), and exploiting election timing for unrelated causes (2 disrupted mass-shooting plots).
insights.so_what: Election-fraud narratives remain the dominant pathway to election violence, raising risk to officials and certifying institutions.
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Election-related terrorism comes from across the spectrum: 6 of 11 incidents right-wing (or 3 of 8 episodes counting Peña's campaign once), 3 left-wing, 1 jihadist, and Brian Cole Jr.'s pipe bombs targeted both parties' headquarters.
insights.so_what: Risk is not attributable to a single movement, complicating partisan framings of political violence.
insights.quote: Election-related terrorism has emerged from several ideological directions rather than from a single movement or political constituency.
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Jihadism was the most common driver of U.S. terrorism from January 2023 to June 2026 with 25 incidents (19 plots, 6 attacks) and 15 deaths, almost all from the January 2025 New Orleans Bourbon Street ramming; jihadists are drawn to crowds and publicity rather than electoral grievances.
insights.so_what: Midterm rallies and election-night gatherings are plausible mass-casualty targets for crowd-seeking jihadists.
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Anti-government extremism produced 21 incidents and four deaths and partisan extremism 8 incidents and three deaths from January 2023 to June 2026; elections focus their hostility on candidates, election workers, courts and party offices.
insights.so_what: Election administrators and certifying bodies are a key vulnerability amid ongoing fraud claims in 2026.
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: With Donald Trump not on the ballot in 2026, some election-related grievances may diminish, since he has been a focal point for terrorism both supporting and opposing him.
insights.so_what: A modest mitigating factor for midterm violence risk relative to presidential cycles.
insights.quote: One potentially mitigating factor is that Trump himself is not on the ballot this election cycle.
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: White supremacist terrorism caused 9 incidents and 11 deaths and accelerationism 8 incidents from January 2023 to June 2026; accelerationists have plotted against officials and electrical substations (Philippi and Takhistov in 2024) to foment collapse, making elections an attractive backdrop.
insights.so_what: Critical infrastructure such as power substations is a recognized accelerationist target, a risk for utilities around politically charged periods.
insights.locator: White Supremacy and AccelerationismWhite supremacist terrorism
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Intense conflict over Israel, Gaza, Iran and U.S. Middle East policy, plus AIPAC involvement in congressional races and more prominent Muslim candidates, could channel antisemitic, anti-Israel and anti-Muslim grievances toward specific 2026 candidates and organizations.
insights.so_what: Foreign-policy conflicts are spilling into domestic electoral security risk.
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Anti-AI and anti-corporate-healthcare extremists have targeted individuals seen as representing industries they oppose, suggesting candidates prominent on those issues could become targets, though incidents are too few to establish patterns.
insights.so_what: Emerging anti-AI and anti-corporate violence is a nascent executive and political security risk to monitor.

themes.theme: Operational profile and effectiveness of security

insights.claim: Only one of the 11 incidents was planned for Election Day itself and none are confirmed to have targeted polling places, ballot counting or election workers; most hit candidates during campaigns or officials after the vote.
insights.so_what: Security must cover the full cycle — campaigns and certification — not just Election Day.
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Nine of 11 incidents reached the attack stage but none killed the intended victims, owing to protective security, perpetrators' limited skills, narrow target sets, and luck; Cole Jr.'s two viable pipe bombs failed only because their timers malfunctioned.
insights.so_what: The zero-fatality record partly reflects luck and may not persist.
insights.quote: None of the 11 incidents succeeded in killing their intended victims.
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: A RAND study found U.S. authorities foiled 31.9 percent of domestic terrorist plots in the six years before 9/11 versus 80.6 percent in the decade after.
insights.so_what: Plots involving extended preparation are usually caught; simple targeted attacks are the residual risk.
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Well-protected prominent targets are comparatively hard to attack successfully, while simple attacks in accessible spaces are hard to prevent; election terrorism mirrors U.S. terrorism broadly — lone male U.S. citizens or small groups using firearms.
insights.so_what: Local candidates and officials with little protection are the most exposed, sustaining demand for protective security services.
insights.quote: prominent political targets with substantial security may be comparatively difficult to attack successfully, while simpler attacks in more accessible spaces may be harder to prevent or disrupt
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Campaigns and officials at all levels have increased protection for 2026 through emergency training, more law enforcement, wider perimeters, controlled entrances, surveillance and bulletproof glass, continuing a multi-year trend.
insights.so_what: Structural growth in political-security spending benefits physical security and surveillance providers.
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Over 40 percent of U.S. politicians said threats made them less willing to run for reelection or higher office, and Swedish research shows even unexposed politicians consider leaving after attacks on others.
insights.so_what: Threats of violence can shrink the candidate pool and alter political outcomes without any attack succeeding.

insights.claim: Attributing individual attacks to whole political movements, as after Routh's attempt on Trump, Peña's shootings, and the killings of Charlie Kirk and Hortman, exaggerates support for violence and can fuel a retaliatory cycle.
insights.so_what: Political violence can feed polarization dynamics that raise policy and institutional uncertainty.

insights.claim: Security responses carry trade-offs: a March 2026 poll showed many but not most Americans favored National Guard monitoring of polling places, which could intimidate voters, and threat-detection could expand into monitoring peaceful civil society.
insights.so_what: Militarized election security could itself become a source of political controversy and lower turnout.

insights.claim: In an unlikely but grave scenario, officials or allies could exploit violence or fear of violence to justify measures that interfere with, delay or discredit an election.
insights.so_what: A low-probability, high-impact governance tail risk for U.S. institutional stability.
